title: Australia Rewrites Skilled Visa Processing Priorities in Two New Ministerial Directions
excerpt: Ministerial Directions 121 and 122, signed on 18 September and in force from 19 September, put construction, healthcare, teaching, agriculture and resources workers at the front of the queue — and end the old penalty for offshore applicants in priority occupations.
body:
• Australia's Immigration Minister Tony Burke signed Ministerial Directions 121 and 122 on 18 September 2026; both commenced on 19 September, replacing the skilled-visa processing priorities under Ministerial Direction 119.
  • Direction 121 sets a five-tier processing queue for temporary skilled visas, chiefly the Subclass 482 Skills in Demand visa; Direction 122 sets a four-tier queue for provisional and permanent skilled visas including subclasses 186, 187, 189, 190, 191, 489, 491, 494, 887 and 888.
  • Workers in construction, healthcare, teaching, agriculture, aquaculture, fishing and resources — plus law enforcement and defence — sit at the front of the queue, and offshore applicants in those sectors are now ranked equally with onshore applicants.
  • The Directions reorder processing queues only: they change no eligibility criteria, create no new visa, and do not guarantee faster decisions or approvals. They also apply to applications lodged before 19 September that had not yet been finally determined.

A new order in the queue

Australia has rewritten the order in which skilled visa applications are processed. Ministerial Directions 121 and 122, signed by Home Affairs and Immigration Minister Tony Burke on 18 September 2026, took effect the next day and replaced the priorities that operated under Ministerial Direction 119, according to the Department of Home Affairs.

Direction 121 covers temporary skilled visas — chiefly the Subclass 482 Skills in Demand visa, which replaced the Temporary Skill Shortage visa in December 2024. Direction 122 covers provisional and permanent skilled visas, including the Employer Nomination Scheme (186), Skilled Independent (189), Skilled Nominated (190), and regional visas such as 491, 494 and 887.

Who moves to the front

Direction 121 ranks Subclass 482 applications in five groups: priority-sector occupations first (onshore and offshore treated equally), then the Specialist Skills stream for applicants earning at least AUD 146,576 a year, then other onshore applicants, then unaccompanied offshore applicants, then everything else. Direction 122 applies the same logic across four groups for provisional and permanent visas, without the Specialist Skills tier.

The named sectors are construction, healthcare, teaching, agriculture, aquaculture, fishing and resources, plus law enforcement and defence. One caution from immigration lawyers: working for an employer in a priority industry does not automatically confer priority — the nominated occupation and position decide the group.

"Processing priority does not mean visa eligibility or visa approval."

— Madhab Kharel, Principal Lawyer, Emigrate Lawyers

What changed from Direction 119

Agriculture, aquaculture, fishing and resources now sit in the top tier; Direction 119 centred on law enforcement, defence, healthcare, teaching and construction. And the offshore penalty is gone — under Direction 119, location affected priority even within priority occupations; now a qualifying applicant gets first priority whether lodging from Sydney or from India.

The definitions have been sharpened: defence now covers AUKUS-related positions, teaching adds Faculty Head, construction adds Engineering Manager, Civil Engineering Draftsperson and Civil Engineering Technician, and healthcare extends to aged and disabled carers and nursing support workers.

What it means for Indian applicants

Australia hosts one of the world's largest Indian communities, and Indians rank among the biggest cohorts of skilled migrants. The offshore-equals-onshore rule directly affects the most common pathway: an Indian professional hired by an Australian employer while still living in India.

The examples are concrete. A mining engineer nominated for a 482 now lands in priority one. A nurse in Bengaluru recruited by a Queensland hospital is no longer ranked behind an equivalent onshore applicant. The Directions also reach backwards — they apply to applications lodged before 19 September that had not yet been finally determined — so pending applicants should check where they now stand.

Priority is not approval

A higher priority does not guarantee a decision by any date, nor approval. Applicants must still meet every requirement — skills assessments, English, health and character checks, sponsorship and salary thresholds — and an incomplete application can still stall in the queue.

Part of a wider migration overhaul

The directions sit within a broader package Burke outlined at the National Press Club on 17 September, covering students, visitor and working holiday visas and aimed at keeping net overseas migration toward 245,000 in 2026–27 and 225,000 in 2027–28. Announced alongside: planned points-test changes weighting construction trades comparably to degrees. Some measures still need implementation, so the fine print will evolve.

What to watch

Applicants should confirm their ANZSCO occupation and nominated position against the new definitions, since the classification decides the queue. Employers recruiting from overseas gain a simpler path in priority sectors. But the bar to clear the queue has not moved — and a better place in line is not a visa in hand.
image_caption: Parliament House in Canberra, Australia. Two new ministerial directions rewrite how skilled visa applications are prioritised.
nri_angle: Australia's large Indian professional community and applicants still in India benefit directly: offshore priority-sector applicants now rank equally with onshore applicants, removing a long-standing disadvantage for Indians hired by Australian employers while living in India.
author: Diaspora Desk
